population.note: FICTIONAL. Base is ≈272M adults. Current users: 24.2% ≈ 65.9M. Ever-used: 33.5% ≈ 91.1M. Used and off now: 9.3% ≈ 25.3M. Never used: ≈181M. Cycling arithmetic in one line: current 24.2 = 7.5 first-course starters from this window + 4.2 continuous first-course users from before 2030 (≈55% two-year persistence among long-tenured users) + 12.5 on a second or later course; the off-now 9.3 = 2.0 new starters already stopped + 3.5 who restarted and stopped again + 3.8 single-course stoppers; so cycled = (12.5 + 3.5) / 33.5 = 48%. Ever-use rose 9.5 points (new starters 7.5 + 2.0). Prior ever-users: 16.7 on + 7.3 off = 24.0, which checks. About 6 of the 9.4 points who were off in 2030 came back, pulled by the widened Medicare Bridge, more Medicaid states and the monthly MariTide. The monthly product raised persistence among new starters: roughly 52% one-year persistence on monthly against ~38% on weekly in gated plans. Age check: 18–29 14% × 51M = 7.1M; 30–49 26.5% × 90M = 23.9M; 50–64 34% × 62M = 21.1M; 65+ 20% × 69M = 13.8M; total 65.9M = 24.2%. The 65+ band jumped from 8.5% to 20% when the Bridge criteria widened, and DEXA-advised pauses still keep it below the 50–64 band. The bottom third rose from 10.3% to 20.5% mostly through Medicaid; imported and counterfeit users fell from ≈3.1M to ≈2.6M after the Chinese API squeeze. Pediatric: 1.3% of ≈73M under-18s ≈ 0.95M, of whom ≈0.18M are aged 6–11 on semaglutide under the 2031 approval and ≈0.77M are adolescents; ≈55% of pediatric users are covered by Medicaid/CHIP through EPSDT. The off-now 25.3M is a visible population of DEXA pausers, gated-plan non-responders, people who quit because of 'the grey', and a shrinking group refusing on principle. The never-used ~181M skew under 30, rural, uninsured, or are people who were never eligible or never interested. About one American child in six now lives with at least one parent currently on an incretin.

access.public_coverage: The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge successor (Nov 2031 agreement, 2032–33) widened eligibility to BMI ≥30 alone or BMI ≥27 with any one weight-related comorbidity, including prediabetes, osteoarthritis and sleep apnea, and added MariTide and amycretin to the formulary. The rate rose from $199 to $245/month-equivalent with tariff and capacity pass-through; the $50 beneficiary copay and the counselling-visit/fall-screening requirement are unchanged. Medicare pays 22.6% of adult fills ≈ 14.9M users (13.4M aged 65+ plus 1.5M disabled under-65), of whom ≈8.4M use the Bridge for obesity. 2032 Bridge spend: 8.4M × $245 × 12 ≈ $24.7B, up from $4.3B in 2030. Medicaid: 38 states plus DC now cover the obesity indication, by state budget decisions using the federal rate rather than any new federal mandate. Medicaid pays 14.0% of adult fills ≈ 9.2M users: 9.2M × $245 × 12 ≈ $27.0B gross federal+state before supplemental rebates. Separately, EPSDT makes Medicaid/CHIP the default payer for ≈0.52M pediatric users. Medicare is now the largest single payer of incretin fills in the US. The Indiana and Arkansas waivers are unchanged.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India: 80+ semaglutide brands at $5–30/month domestically, but export pens now carry a CDSCO export-certification surcharge, and delivered mail-order prices to the US run $60–120. China: domestic generics continue; the Jan 2031 peptide-API export licensing regime cut gray-trade volume and roughly tripled the delivered price of Chinese vials. Canada: generic semaglutide at CAD 60–90/month. EU: first generic semaglutide approvals in 2031–32 in several member states. Brazil, Mexico and Turkey: generics. Oral semaglutide generics are sold in most non-US markets.
access.note: FICTIONAL. Price shock up. Three mechanisms. (1) The Jan 2031 Chinese API export licensing regime: delivered gray vials went from ~$30 to $90–150. (2) The Aug 2031 sterility failure and recall at a contract fill-finish plant: retatrutide and the higher tirzepatide doses were on the FDA shortage list until Jan 2032. (3) The Nov 2031 renewal of the direct-portal and Bridge prices passed through Section 232 tariff and capacity costs. Direct-portal prices from Jan 2032: injectable semaglutide $249 (was $199); tirzepatide $279–329 (was $199–279); higher oral doses $219 (was $199); oral starting doses $179 (was $149); retatrutide $499 direct (was $399), list $1,599 (was $1,499); MariTide $449 direct, $1,250 list. Wegovy list is still $1,349. PBM net under outcome contracts rose from ≈$170–190 to ≈$225–260. Payer mix of ≈65.9M adult users: commercial 40.0% (26.4M), Medicare 22.6% (14.9M), Medicaid 14.0% (9.2M), cash/direct 19.5% (12.85M, including ≈3.0M 'calm'/'craving freedom' subscribers), imported/counterfeit 3.9% (2.6M); total 100% ≈ 65.9M. About 75% of covering employers gate. Monthly MariTide makes the ≥80% PDC rule trivial to meet, and some PBMs now prefer it for that reason. The 503B exclusion and 503A injunction stand; compounders' attempt to use the 2031 shortage listing was rejected in court under the existing injunction. Personal-importation enforcement is unchanged: seizures and warnings, no prosecution of individuals.

on_market_classes: GLP-1 agonist, weekly injectable (semaglutide: Wegovy/Ozempic, incl. 7.2 mg; Wegovy now labelled for ages 6+)
GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1 + amylin analogue combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema)
GLP-1/amylin unimolecular agonist, weekly injectable (amycretin, approved Sep 2031)
GLP-1 agonist / GIPR antagonist antibody-peptide conjugate, monthly injectable (maridebart cafraglutide: MariTide, approved Jun 2031)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill, Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: pediatric obesity ages 6–11 (semaglutide, Mar 2031, with bone-accrual and growth postmarketing requirements)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: 'calm' and 'craving freedom' subscriptions (low-dose oral semaglutide or Foundayo, $179–219/month) for people without obesity, ≈3.0M subscribers; marketing has softened after FTC letters, but the product line has grown
smoking and vaping cessation (still off-label; new Novo trial with anhedonia endpoints under way)
longevity and 'metabolic health' regimens in concierge practices
pediatric use under 6 under specialist care (rare)
'micro-dosing' or 'half-shot' MariTide schedules to soften the grey, against label
drugs.pipeline_note: FICTIONAL. MariTide (Amgen, filed Apr 2030) was approved in Jun 2031 as the first monthly incretin, with a DEXA substudy in its label and a bone postmarketing requirement. It realises the monthly driver; supply ramped through 2032 to ≈5.5M users. There is no implant on the US market. Amycretin was approved in Sep 2031 after the 72-week DEXA data. Survodutide's resubmission (Feb 2032) is under review, with a decision expected in 2033. Bimagrumab-plus-semaglutide was filed in Mar 2032 and cannot be approved before Mar 2033. Semaglutide received the six-month pediatric exclusivity grant tied to its 6–11 studies, and a patent settlement announced in Apr 2031 sets the earliest US generic semaglutide entry at Apr 2033, so there is no US generic in this window. Tirzepatide exclusivity runs to the mid-2030s. Bone agents are standard companions for long-term users over 50. Incretin market ≈$152B in 2032: US volume up ~67% since 2030 and US net price up ~10–20% after the shock, while ex-US revenue keeps eroding to generics.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the most common class effect and the leading cause of voluntary discontinuation. MariTide's first-dose vomiting is front-loaded and lasts longer per episode because the drug cannot be stopped quickly. Low-dose escalation schedules are now standard.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; the severe gastroparesis caution is retained; MariTide label carries a titration schedule.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Elevated with rapid loss. Absolute case counts rise in proportion to the larger user base; no change in rate.
Still no causal confirmation; absolute risk low. Counterfeit-product cases still confound reporting.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; MDL litigation ongoing, with no bellwether verdict.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Unchanged rates: lean-mass loss is ~30–40% of weight lost in untrained users over 50. With 65+ use more than doubling, the absolute number of sarcopenic long-term users roughly doubles too.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: The 2028 class label and the 2029 joint guidance are retained. The Medicare counselling visit is retained and now includes a strength-referral checkbox. No statute.

safety_ledger.effect: Bone mineral density loss and fragility fracture
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No new signal; the ledger holds and only the scale changes. HR ~1.3–1.4 in 65+ long-term users and ~1.2 in postmenopausal women aged 50–64 with repeated cycling. ≈5.0M 65+ users on >2 years × ~0.6%/yr baseline × 0.35 excess ≈ 10,500 excess hip fractures a year, against ~310,000 total. DEXA waits of 10–14 weeks are common in Sun Belt metros.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelling and the 2029 guidance are retained. FDA required DEXA data for the MariTide and amycretin approvals. The DOJ civil case against Novo is unresolved.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohort studies still conflict; absolute risk very low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label; FDA warnings mention; no class determination.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association; nothing new in the pediatric 6–11 data.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia, 'the grey')
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No new data class. Retatrutide SHAPS findings are unchanged (~10–14% of top-dose users vs ~5%). Complaints are now common in primary care. MariTide users report a monthly cycle, flattest around days 7–14, and cannot take a quick holiday because the drug's long half-life means a skipped dose takes ~6 weeks to wash out.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No label change. FTC enforcement against advertising claims continues. Novo's smoking-cessation re-trial includes SHAPS.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Substantial regain within a year. Involuntary stops from gated plans continue. Regain after MariTide is delayed by weeks because of the drug's long half-life but is not prevented.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None directly. The Indiana waiver case is still pending in the Seventh Circuit.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Iron, B12, vitamin D, calcium and protein insufficiency signals persist in high-loss and older users. Pediatric dietitians now monitor growth-relevant intake in children on the drug.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Professional guidance (2029) is retained; the AAP issued 2031 nutrition monitoring advice for under-12 users; no FDA action.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~9 years; pediatric and adolescent exposure; repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About ten years of follow-up now. The interim adolescent bone-accrual report (2032) found no statistically significant difference at 2 years but was underpowered. Under-12 exposure is now ~1.5 years at most. Cycling still looks worse for bone than continuous use.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Pediatric bone-accrual and growth postmarketing requirements attached to the 6–11 approval; final reports due 2035.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit / imported product harms (dosing errors, contamination, substitution)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Plateauing. Poison-centre calls are flat in 2031–32 as the Chinese API squeeze cut volume, but the 2031 shortage briefly revived counterfeit retatrutide sales. No insulin-substitution cluster on the scale of 2029.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Import alerts, seizures and pen-authentication guidance continue; no prosecution of individuals; no new law.

safety_ledger.effect: Falls and frailty-related injury in older users
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Fall-related ED visits remain elevated in 65+ users with >2 years' use. Absolute counts rise with Bridge expansion; confounding is still not separated.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Fall-risk screening remains in the Bridge counselling template.

food_and_beverage.state: With nearly a quarter of adults on the drug, US salty-snack volume is falling ~4–5% a year and sugary drinks ~3–4%. Confectionery is shifting to single-bite formats. School-food vendors are reformulating as pediatric prescribing spreads, and two major snack companies sold their legacy cookie brands to private equity in 2032. Protein, fibre and 'bone-forward' lines are still the growth engines. The heritage 'full portion' niche is shrinking as backlash fades.

alcohol.state: US spirits volume has fallen for five straight years, and beer is down too. 'Calm' subscriptions keep eroding occasional drinking. Non-alcoholic and 'one good drink' premium formats carry the on-premise trade. Tobacco and vape volumes fall faster than pre-incretin trends.

restaurants.state: Traffic is flat to slightly down and spend per cover is lower. Half portions are the default, and menus print protein grams. Value buffets keep closing. The Atlanta and Memphis 'no-gram' rooms survive but have stopped growing as their political edge dulls. Chains discover a 'shot week' pattern: monthly users eat noticeably more in the final week of the cycle.

apparel.state: Size churn continues, but the monthly product and the bigger 65+ cohort steady it; fewer people swing fast. Extended petite-and-tall-older ranges grow. Plus-size specialists consolidate, and one major chain closed in 2031.

fitness.state: Still growing. Prescribed strength training is standard for Bridge users. Senior strength gyms in Phoenix, Tampa and The Villages run waitlists, and MA plans pay for them. Mobile DEXA vans are common.

insurance.state: The price shock pushed PBM net from ≈$170–190 to ≈$225–260. Employer coverage slipped from 63% to 61%, and gating rose to ~75% of covering employers. Pharmacy trend is back to ~+9%. Insurers welcome Medicare's growth as the payer of last resort for older members and ask retirees to move to the Bridge. MariTide's monthly dosing lowers gating churn.

pharma.state: Lilly still dominates US volume. Amgen's MariTide is the fastest launch in the class by persistence, constrained by supply. Novo uses the six months of pediatric exclusivity and the 2033 settlement to hold semaglutide share in Medicare and pediatrics. The recalling contract manufacturer is under a consent-decree negotiation. Bone-agent and DEXA suppliers keep growing.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Being on it is unremarkable, like a statin. Being off now needs explaining, and the explanations are standardised: 'bones', 'my plan dropped me', 'the grey'. Visible regain reads as a coverage problem, not a moral one. In suburban Plano and Mesa the 'on it too long' stoop is common enough among retirees that it no longer marks anyone.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The level gap narrowed: bottom 20.5% against top 27%. The quality gap persists. Top-third users get DEXA, coaching and dose tuning. Bottom-third users get Medicaid at the federal rate with a pharmacy kiosk weigh-in and a 10–14-week scan wait. Rural uninsured adults under 30 are now the clearest 'never on it' group.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Holiday tables plan for 'on' and 'off', and 'off-by-conviction' has mostly folded back into 'off'. Kids' birthday parties in pediatric-heavy districts serve half-size cupcakes. Families in Columbus and Phoenix with a parent and a child both on the drug describe dinner as 'protein first, then whatever's left'.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: On/off is stated less on profiles because 'on' is assumed. 'Unmedicated' survives as a filter in small communities. The MariTide 'shot week' is now a dating-app joke, as in 'don't judge me in week two'.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite is a managed variable. The 2030 backlash coalition has thinned: the Atlanta body-sovereignty collectives persist as a cultural voice, the Tulsa–Dallas congregations quietly accepted the pediatric approval as 'medicine for the children', and supplement sellers pivoted to 'GLP-1 support' stacks for people on the drug. Refusal is now a personal stance more than a movement.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL. Measurement has not changed: the retatrutide SHAPS data (~10–14% of top-dose users vs ~5%) remain the only near-RCT-grade figure. Complaint is now ordinary. A May 2032 national survey has 38% of current users reporting at least one deliberate dose holiday or self-reduction in the past year, and 1 in 4 MariTide users describing a recognisable 'grey week'. Among the ≈3.0M 'calm' subscribers, vendor-reported churn has risen to ~45%/year as satisfaction claims meet ordinary experience.
interior_life.framing: A side effect everyone knows about, managed like statin aches. 'The grey' is household vocabulary. Clinicians offer 'dose tuning'. Wellness brands have moved from 'Quiet' to 'Tunable', selling app-guided low-dose titration.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Dose holidays before high-stakes days are normal and tolerated in sales, hospitality and creative jobs. Gated plans still punish holidays that drop PDC below 80%, which weekly users work around by taking short holidays. Monthly MariTide users can't, so some employers' HR guides mention 'shot timing' for performance reviews. Fleet drivers stay on for DOT reasons.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: 'Written unmedicated' is no longer a selling point because so many artists openly say they take holidays to write. Nashville's off-dose scene has become a scheduling practice, with 'holiday sessions'. Extreme-stimulus leisure stays elevated. A 2032 sitcom built around a couple out of sync on their monthly shots is a hit.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Couples sync dose holidays or shot dates. Sex therapists routinely ask which week of the cycle a complaint falls in. Some couples on MariTide align their injection dates so their grey weeks coincide, and others deliberately offset them.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: In the 2032 election year incretins are a cost-of-living issue: the January price step-up, the Bridge's $24.7B, and Medicaid budgets. Both parties claim the Bridge expansion. The grey shows up as a talk-show topic, not a policy. Pollsters still find no measurable temperament effect on turnout, and campaigns quietly schedule rallies with no regard for shot weeks.

state.regulatory_posture: Continuation; no new state action. The FDA demands bone data and gets it: MariTide and amycretin were approved with DEXA labelling, and survodutide is still pending. The pediatric 6–11 approval follows the existing pathway with postmarketing requirements. Import enforcement is unchanged. The FTC still acts only on claims.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No mandate. Public expansion runs through the existing CMS–manufacturer agreement mechanism (Nov 2031 Bridge renewal with widened criteria) and state Medicaid budget choices, at a higher $245 rate. EPSDT makes Medicaid the default pediatric payer without new law.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Unchanged in kind: the Indiana and Arkansas waivers, wellness surcharges up to 30% of premium, PBM outcome gating, and pharmacy weigh-in kiosks. The scale is bigger because more Medicaid states contract the same kiosk networks for verification, though only the two waiver states impose lockouts.
state.workforce_or_military: DOT sleep-apnea screening still nudges drivers toward tirzepatide. Army accession policy on GLP-1 use is unchanged and contested; recruiters report more applicants with pediatric-era exposure. Fleets keep DEXA screening for drivers over 55.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: China's Jan 2031 peptide-API export licensing is framed in Beijing as quality control and in Washington as leverage. India negotiates export certification as a trade concession. The Aug 2031 domestic fill-finish failure exposed how few US sterile-injectable lines exist, and the Nov 2031 price renewal was partly bargained around capacity credits. Section 232 tariffs remain.

events.event: China imposes export licensing on peptide APIs and finished incretin pens, citing counterfeit scandals; delivered prices for mail-order vials to the US roughly triple and US gray-market volume falls by about a sixth

FDA approves Wegovy for children aged 6–11 with obesity, with bone-accrual and growth studies required; Novo receives six months of pediatric exclusivity and, weeks later, settles patent litigation setting the earliest US generic semaglutide entry at April 2033
FDA approves Amgen's MariTide, the first once-monthly obesity injection, with DEXA results in the label; early PBM data show monthly users clearing adherence gates far more often than weekly users

Sterility failures at a contract fill-finish plant trigger a recall of retatrutide and high-dose tirzepatide autoinjector lots; both go on the FDA shortage list until January, and counterfeit retatrutide briefly reappears online

CMS and manufacturers renew the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge for 2032–33 with broader eligibility and new monthly products, but at $245 a month instead of $199; direct-portal prices rise $30–100 from January, citing tariffs and capacity costs

National survey finds most adults now consider GLP-1 use 'as ordinary as a statin', while 38% of users report a deliberate dose holiday in the past year and 'the grey' tops a list of primary-care complaints

open_tensions: Public spending has jumped: the Bridge costs ≈$24.7B and Medicaid ≈$27.0B gross in 2032 at the higher $245 rate. That is the 2033 budget fight, made sharper by generic semaglutide entry in April 2033, which could cut costs or set off a new price war.

Monthly MariTide fits adherence gates and the bone guidance poorly: it makes PDC easy to meet but a DEXA-advised pause slow to take effect, and it turns the familiar dose holiday into a six-week commitment.
Nearly a million children are on incretins, about 180k of them under 12, with no final bone-accrual or growth data until 2035, and Medicaid is their default payer.
The price shock pushed cash and gray buyers toward public programs and gated plans. The 2.6M still on imported product are the people least likely to get a DEXA scan or a pharmacist's check.
still_true: No FDA-approved generic semaglutide or tirzepatide exists in the US; semaglutide entry is now set for no earlier than April 2033.
Wegovy's list price remains $1,349 a month, and almost nobody pays it.
The Medicare Bridge beneficiary copay remains $50 a month, and the counselling-visit requirement is retained.

The Indiana and Arkansas Medicaid 1115 waivers still require ≥80% proportion-of-days-covered and quarterly verified weigh-ins; two misses end coverage for 12 months, and the disability-rights litigation is still unresolved.
The suicidal-ideation warning removed from Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels in January 2026 has not returned.

prose.headline: Nobody Asks If You're On It Anymore. They Ask Why You Stopped, and What Week of the Shot You're In.
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2032 almost one American adult in four is on an incretin drug, and the country has stopped finding this interesting. People talk about the shot the way their parents talked about statins. Someone on it is not news. Someone off it gets a polite question, and the answers are now familiar: bones, the plan dropped me, the grey.

The increase happened while prices went up, and how it happened explains the world. In January 2031 China put export licences on peptide ingredients, and the mail-order vials that had supplied three million Americans tripled in price overnight. In August a contract plant that fills autoinjectors failed a sterility inspection. Retatrutide and the higher tirzepatide doses spent five months on the shortage list. In November, when the government and the manufacturers renewed their pricing deal, the cheap era ended. The direct-portal shot that cost $199 went to $249, the starter pills went to $179, and Medicare's rate went to $245. It also became broader than ever. Since January almost anyone over sixty-five with a BMI of thirty, or twenty-seven with sore knees or borderline blood sugar, qualifies for a $50 copay. Medicare now pays for more incretin fills than any other single payer. Thirty-eight states cover the drug through Medicaid. Squeezed cash buyers and gray-market buyers moved into public programs, so the price shock ended up on the government's books. That is about $25 billion for the Medicare Bridge this year and another $27 billion gross for Medicaid, in an election year.

The other driver was the calendar. In June 2031 Amgen's MariTide became the first once-a-month obesity injection. Employers' benefit managers liked it right away, because a person who takes one shot a month easily meets an eighty-percent adherence rule. Persistence went up and fewer people were cut off. Doctors liked it less. A drug that lasts for weeks cannot be paused quickly when a bone scan comes back bad, and it cannot be skipped for a weekend.

That matters because the flattening everyone used to whisper about is now a routine complaint. In a spring survey, nearly four in ten users said they had deliberately taken a dose holiday in the past year. Primary-care doctors offer 'dose tuning' the way they once adjusted blood-pressure pills. Monthly users describe a cycle: queasy at first, flattest in the second week, nearly themselves by the end. A sitcom about a married couple whose shot dates don't line up is a hit. The wellness brands that sold 'Quiet' to people who were never heavy now sell 'Tunable', and nearly half of their subscribers quit each year.

In March 2031 the FDA approved Wegovy for children as young as six. Medicaid's children's benefit, which covers whatever is medically necessary, made the public programme their default payer without anyone passing a law. About 180,000 children under twelve are on it, and nearly a million under eighteen. An interim bone study in teenagers found nothing alarming and was too small to be sure. The final answers are due in 2035. The pediatric approval also gave Novo six more months of exclusivity, and a settlement now keeps generic semaglutide out of the US until April 2033.

Nothing new went wrong this window. The fracture risk is what it was, and there are simply more people to break. About ten thousand extra hip fractures a year now come from long-term users over sixty-five. DEXA waits in Phoenix run three months. The protest coalition that marched in Atlanta in 2030 has mostly gone home. The churches in Tulsa quietly accepted the drug for children, and the supplement sellers now market to people who are on it. Snacks, spirits and buffets keep shrinking slowly. Gyms full of seventy-year-olds doing trap-bar deadlifts keep growing. From outside, it all looks well managed.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Ray Delgado wakes at five because forty years of HVAC calls in the Mesa heat trained him to. It is the eleventh, which means shot day. He keeps the MariTide pen in the butter compartment, which is otherwise empty because Lorraine stopped buying butter in 2029. He pinches his belly, counts, and feels the cold. It cost fifty dollars on the Medicare card, same as always. In January the pharmacist told him the government now pays two hundred forty-five for it, as if that were his business.

Lorraine is off. Her DEXA came back with a number the doctor didn't like, so now she gets the yearly infusion, eats a whole tortilla again, and tells people at church 'Bones' before they can ask. Everyone nods. Nobody asks Ray anything.

At ten he drives his granddaughter Mia, who is nine, to the clinic on Southern Avenue for her weigh-in. She is on the kids' Wegovy through AHCCCS, and the nurse calls her a rockstar. Three other mothers in the waiting room carry the same little orange sharps box. Afterward Mia asks for a churro. He says yes, then watches her eat half and hand him the rest.

At the senior gym the coach puts him on the trap bar. He doesn't love it, but he doesn't love much lately. He used to hate traffic, the Suns and his brother-in-law, and now all of it is fine. Day one is the queasy one. The quiet comes in about a week, and Lorraine says by day twenty-five he's almost himself.

He once asked Dr. Pham whether he could skip a month. She said he could, but his body wouldn't notice for six weeks.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Medicare is now the largest single payer of incretin fills in the US.
least_plausible_claims.why: Fails magnitude: the candidate's own payer mix gives commercial 40.0% (26.4M) against Medicare 22.6% (14.9M), so the claim contradicts the reconciliation it sits beside.

least_plausible_claims.quote: About one American child in six now lives with at least one parent currently on an incretin.
least_plausible_claims.why: Fails magnitude: with 26.5% of 30–49-year-olds on the drug, even perfectly correlated couples give at least ~25% of children, and independent parents give ~45%, so one in six does not follow from the age-band data.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Squeezed cash buyers and gray-market buyers moved into public programs, so the price shock ended up on the government's books.
least_plausible_claims.why: Fails mechanism: the world state shows cash/direct users rising from ≈7.9M to 12.85M at an unchanged ~20% share after the price rise, and gray users fell only 0.5M, so the shift into public programs is asserted rather than shown.

rationale.badness: About 24% of adults are on the drug, ~10,500 excess hip fractures a year, 75% of employers gate, and ~1M children are on it with bone and growth data not due until 2035 (population, safety_ledger, open_tensions). Monthly MariTide makes pauses slow and takes away the quick dose holiday, and DEXA waits run 10–14 weeks. Normalisation, a thinning backlash and a named, discussable 'grey' keep this a harder but legible society, not a catastrophe; the quality gap by class persists, and public spending reaches ~$52B.
rationale.plausibility: driver_fidelity: All ten drivers show up in fields and events: +9.6pp adoption, shock_up, public expansion, pediatric 6–11 approval, monthly MariTide with no implant, normalisation and mainstream complaint.
